title: Who Should Control England's Money? Mayors, Taxes and Regional Inequality
label: 15 September 2026 · England's local funding powers
summary: The House of Lords Economic Affairs Committee questioned representatives of London and Tees Valley about giving regional mayors more control over public money. Both witnesses supported greater local freedom to invest, borrow and plan for economic growth, but they disagreed about how to protect poorer regions. London's Howard Dawber argued that areas should keep a meaningful share of the extra taxes generated by local growth, while Tees Valley Mayor Lord Houchen warned that this could widen existing inequalities unless money was redistributed fairly. The discussion also examined whether new funding would genuinely increase local independence, how borrowing should work, whether mayors were gaining too much power over councils, and whether smaller regions had the staff and expertise to use their new responsibilities effectively. Neither witness offered a complete solution to regional inequality, and important details of the Government's proposals remained undecided.

glossary.definition: Giving local or regional governments greater control over public money, including taxes, spending and borrowing.
A tax paid on most commercial properties, such as shops, offices and factories.
A local tax charged to visitors staying overnight in accommodation such as hotels.
A sum of money provided by central government that an authority can spend with relatively few restrictions.
An organisation through which several neighbouring councils work together on regional responsibilities, often led by an elected mayor.
The UK government department responsible for public finances, taxation and government spending.
A fixed limit on how much money an organisation is allowed to borrow.
The public organisation responsible for London's major transport networks, including the Underground, buses and some rail services.
Value Added Tax, a tax added to the price of many goods and services.
Adjusting how public money is shared so that poorer areas can receive support despite raising less tax locally.
An elected body that questions the Mayor of London, investigates decisions and can challenge the mayor's budget.
Local councils responsible for nearly all council services in their area, rather than sharing responsibilities between two levels of council.
Technology that captures carbon dioxide from industrial processes or power generation and stores it underground to prevent its release.

chapters.title: 1. Would Local Control Help the Economy?
chapters.takeaway: Both witnesses favour giving mayors more freedom over spending, although Houchen warns that the proposed reform may mostly replace existing grants rather than provide genuinely new money.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We're looking at fiscal devolution: giving regional leaders more control over public money. Would that help your local economies grow?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Yes. London's Elizabeth line is a good example. Businesses knew the railway would make new development possible, and some were willing to pay extra taxes towards building it. We eventually created ways to collect that money, but getting government approval took years. If London's mayor had already had those powers, we could have moved much faster.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: The Elizabeth line has been enormously successful. I understand it now carries one in six UK rail passengers, and development around its stations has grown significantly. Future projects could benefit from similar local powers. A visitor levy on overnight stays could raise additional money, while a reliable share of income tax could help mayors borrow to fund major investments.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I agree that more freedom will help, but we need to be precise about what's proposed. This isn't necessarily fiscal devolution in the full sense. Mayors wouldn't suddenly be collecting and setting their own income taxes. The Government is largely talking about changing how it provides the money we already receive.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Take a hypothetical example. Suppose Tees Valley gets £1 billion in government grants over three years. The Government might calculate that this equals a certain share of local income tax, then replace those restricted grants with one block grant. The mayor could choose how to spend it, but that doesn't mean we'd receive additional money or control the actual tax.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: If it's simply £1 billion replacing £1 billion, much of that money is already committed. There may be little left for new projects. But being able to move money between transport, business development and other priorities would help enormously. If a railway project is delayed, for example, we could use the money elsewhere instead of being trapped by government restrictions.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: The other big advantage is certainty. Rather than receiving separate funding agreements lasting three years, mayors could have reliable funding for 10, 15 or 20 years. That's much better for planning roads, industrial sites and other major projects. We'd still have to justify our spending and answer to local voters.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Beyond flexibility and longer-term planning, would these changes make regional government more accountable and effective?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: I think so. At present, about 93% of taxes raised in London go to national government, which decides how much comes back. Cities elsewhere in the world control much more of their own money. If people can see which local taxes are being collected, what their mayor spends them on and what gets delivered, they can judge those decisions more directly.

chapters.title: 2. Borrowing Money and Choosing Taxes
chapters.takeaway: Reliable tax income could help mayors finance projects, but borrowing limits and whether an investment can generate enough money to repay a loan may matter just as much.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Cookham
turns.text: You've suggested that mayors could borrow more if they received income tax rather than government grants. But governments don't simply stop funding local authorities, and they can change tax rates too. Is income tax really a more dependable source of money?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: For many mayors, the important thing is being able to borrow more. Combined authorities have borrowing caps that ordinary councils don't have in quite the same way. I could present an excellent project with reliable income to repay the loan, but if we'd reached our borrowing cap, we couldn't take it forward.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Cookham
turns.text: That's an argument about removing borrowing limits, though. It's different from saying that income tax is more dependable than government funding.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: That's fair. I don't have a strong view on which is more secure. We've already borrowed against government funding guaranteed over 30 years. Treasury officials are also considering protecting mayors if local income tax falls sharply, perhaps because a major employer closes. But they might also limit how much extra tax income successful areas can keep. These are discussions, not settled policy.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: We believe lenders would be more willing to lend against a dependable tax income. Transport for London has already borrowed against future passenger fares to help fund Crossrail. We'd like similar options for projects such as extending the Docklands Light Railway to Thamesmead, including borrowing against future business rates without needing separate Treasury approval.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: There's another distinction. Some investments generate enough money to pay for themselves, without relying on income tax. On Teesside, the South Korean company SeAH made a £1.4 billion investment in a major factory. We retained the business rates from the site and received rental income. Alongside commercial and government-backed support, those income sources helped us arrange private financing for the project.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: But not everything pays for itself. Take subsidised buses. Greater Manchester's Bee Network costs taxpayers around £250 million a year after its income is taken into account. That's a legitimate political choice, but lenders can't expect the service to repay a loan from profits. Borrowing for something like that ultimately depends on public money continuing to support it.

turns.speaker: Lord Petitgas
turns.text: If mayors are going to receive money from local taxes, which taxes make the most sense? What should guide that decision?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: I'd use four tests. Does the tax bring in more money when the local economy grows? Is the income reasonably stable? Can we identify where it's raised? And can residents see how their money is spent? That would reward mayors for improving their economies while making their decisions easier to judge.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Income tax and business rates meet many of those tests. A visitor levy is also straightforward because you know which hotels collect it. VAT is harder: if someone buys something online, it's not always obvious which area should receive the tax. We'd favour starting with taxes that can clearly be linked to a particular place.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Broadly, I agree. Keeping business rates has been very valuable in Teesside. We're expecting substantial future revenue from businesses at Teesworks, the redevelopment of the former steelworks site. But there's a danger. When old industries decline and factories close, an area can lose a huge amount of tax income. Poorer regions could face another financial crisis through no fault of their mayors.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: National decisions about electricity prices, regulation and employment costs can overwhelm what we achieve locally. We might attract major investment and thousands of jobs, then lose jobs elsewhere because businesses can't afford to operate. Any new tax arrangements must recognise that local leaders don't control the whole economy.

chapters.title: 3. How Do We Stop Richer Regions Pulling Further Ahead?
chapters.takeaway: Dawber wants regions to keep the gains from future growth, while Houchen argues that historical disadvantages must be addressed before those rewards can be shared fairly.

turns.speaker: Lord Prentis of Leeds
turns.text: If areas get to keep more tax when their economies grow, what happens to places that struggle? How do we reward success without making poorer areas worse off?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: We need equalisation, but we shouldn't treat this as though one area can benefit only if another loses. My starting point would be that no area gets less money on the day the new system begins. Replace an amount of government grant with the same amount of local tax income, then let areas keep a meaningful share of any extra tax generated by future growth.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: The danger is that our starting positions are very different. Three per cent of income tax in Tees Valley would raise about £170 million a year, compared with roughly £2.3 billion in London. Without money being redistributed, we'd be locking existing inequalities into the system. But if government compensates unsuccessful areas for every loss, those areas may have less incentive to improve.

turns.speaker: Lord Prentis of Leeds
turns.text: So how much equalisation is needed, and how should it actually work?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: I'd protect the starting level of funding and let places retain a share of the growth above that level. The arrangement should last long enough to make investment worthwhile. I'd suggest around 10 years before the starting figures are reviewed. If everything is recalculated every two or three years, councils and mayors could lose the financial reward just as their investments start succeeding.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: We'd also need protection against national decisions. If the Chancellor cuts income tax for the whole country, that shouldn't automatically reduce money promised to mayors. And essential services such as policing and fire protection should have separate funding arrangements, so a sudden economic downturn doesn't put them at risk.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: There's a bigger question about what kind of country we want. Teesside has suffered from decades of industrial decline and decisions made by successive governments. If we believe everyone should have a fair opportunity, stronger areas must help weaker ones. I don't think national government would actually stand aside and let a struggling region run out of money.

turns.speaker: Lord Burns
turns.text: Suppose these tax arrangements had existed for the last 25 years. Would regional inequality be better or worse today?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: In Teesside, we'd probably have suffered a serious financial collapse during the decline of the chemical and processing industries. We would have lost enormous amounts of business rates. Later, rebuilding the former Redcar steelworks site could have transformed our finances. That's exactly the problem: the money could rise and fall dramatically, and government would face pressure to rescue us during the bad years.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: London's experience might have been different. We had worthwhile transport and housing projects ready years ago that central government couldn't prioritise. If we'd been able to borrow and invest ourselves, some could have happened much earlier. I also think elected mayors have already made a difference. Without a Mayor of London, I doubt we'd have had the Elizabeth line or perhaps even the Olympics.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: Are you worried that these changes could end up penalising London if growth elsewhere doesn't materialise?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: No, I'm reasonably confident. London and the rest of Britain aren't separate economies. Businesses based in London employ people and manufacture goods elsewhere, and businesses outside London benefit from connections to London. We shouldn't choose between London growing and the regions growing. We need both.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: London contributed a net £49 billion to the rest of the UK's public finances last year, according to our figures. We'd like that contribution to increase. If more local freedom helps London grow faster, national government can also collect more money to invest in the rest of the country.

turns.speaker: Lord Newby
turns.text: But there's a disagreement here. Howard wants everyone to begin with their present funding. Ben says the north has been disadvantaged for decades. Wouldn't keeping the current starting position preserve that disadvantage?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Yes. Teesside has to benefit from money raised in stronger areas such as London. Otherwise, when London begins with £2.3 billion and we begin with £170 million, how could we realistically catch up? We don't yet know how much redistribution the Government proposes, so there will inevitably be arguments about what each region receives.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: My point is that we should preserve current overall funding when we switch from grants to local tax income, rather than simply handing each area all the tax collected there. Then we should reward additional growth. If you take away every extra pound an area earns, there's little financial benefit for it to invest.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But different regions face very different challenges. Teesside has an industrial history that makes its economic transition harder than somewhere like Manchester. Doesn't that complicate any simple formula?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Absolutely. Some mayors believe every area should keep whatever it generates, but I fundamentally disagree. Poor communities can be hit much harder by national economic shocks. Government will probably have to keep adjusting the balance between regions as circumstances change. There's no easy formula that permanently removes that political choice.

chapters.title: 4. Should Mayors or Local Councils Be in Charge?
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses see benefits in regional leadership, but Houchen warns that giving mayors ever more responsibilities could weaken local councils and distract mayors from economic development.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: We're discussing handing more powers to mayors and regional authorities. But what about ordinary local councils? Shouldn't they receive some of these powers themselves?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: London works differently from many other regions. The mayor and borough councils are separate organisations, but we work closely together. Councils are under enormous pressure from adult social care and temporary housing costs, leaving little money for other services. Their funding needs attention too, but that can be considered alongside giving regional authorities more control.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Government policy is clearly favouring regional mayors over councils. We've even seen funding for homelessness directed to regional authorities, although local councils have the staff and experience to deliver that help. So we receive the money and pass it on to them.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I don't believe directly elected mayors necessarily create a democratic problem. In my experience, more people recognise their mayor than their council leader. Mayors are elected every four years and can be voted out. But there is confusion about what we actually control, and what remains the responsibility of councils or national government.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: People still expect their councils to collect bins, repair local roads and deal with neighbourhood problems. My concern is that we're gradually creating regional governments that can dictate to councils. Have we properly considered what that means for local democracy?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: I don't think mayors should replace councils. Some responsibilities clearly belong nationally, such as defence. Major transport, economic planning and programmes connecting people with jobs across a whole city make sense regionally. Bin collections, local parks and libraries belong locally. The important thing is knowing who should do what.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: For example, someone living in Tower Hamlets might need training in Newham to take a job in Westminster. London's mayor can help coordinate that across borough boundaries. That doesn't mean taking control of every council service.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I'm unusual among mayors on this. I think our relatively narrow responsibilities have helped us succeed. We were created mainly to attract investment, create jobs and improve the transport and training needed for economic growth. My message to government is: don't keep giving us more different responsibilities. Give us stronger powers over the things we already do.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: There's an argument for adding almost anything. If jobs matter, we supposedly need to control healthcare so people are fit to work, and police because crime affects investment. Soon mayors could be running organisations that resemble enormous local councils. I worry about responsibilities moving upwards from councils instead of downwards from central government.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: Housing seems particularly sensitive. Regional planning is understandable, but whether a particular park or factory site should become housing is a very local decision.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: I agree that detailed decisions should remain local. London sets an overall housing and planning policy and helps councils with major developments. We examine around 200 large planning proposals each year, but we don't intervene in most of them.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Outside London, the Government wants regional mayors to produce plans identifying suitable areas for housing and industry. Councils would then have to follow those plans when making their own. Mayors may also gain powers to review or overturn certain rejected developments.

chapters.title: 5. Planning Decisions and Checks on Mayors
chapters.takeaway: Stronger planning powers might help housing and industry develop faster, but they could also create conflict with councils and raise questions about transparency and public participation.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: If regional and local authorities have overlapping responsibilities, won't there be constant disagreements? And isn't planning, especially the power to overrule councils, likely to be a major source of conflict?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I think conflict is inevitable. Originally, many mayoral decisions required agreement from local council leaders. Budget decisions even needed everyone to agree, though that's since been changed to a majority. Increasingly, we're seeing powers that mayors can exercise without council approval. That's a significant change in how regional government works.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: London shows that different levels of government can work together. We developed our economic growth plan jointly with the borough councils, so they helped decide what it should contain. Planning also works through a citywide plan, with local councils making detailed decisions within it. Political disagreements happen, but cooperation can still be very effective.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Since 2008, London's mayor has been able to approve certain developments rejected by councils, as well as stop some that councils support. I think that has generally worked well. Outside London, national ministers already have powers to take over major planning decisions. I'd rather see an accountable regional mayor making decisions about their own area.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I'm expecting some friction in Teesside. Councils have rejected housing schemes that professional planners supported, only for those schemes to be approved later after an appeal. I'd use the proposed powers to help get sensible developments built. If people think I've made the wrong decisions, they can vote me out.

turns.speaker: Lord Burns
turns.text: But if you can make these decisions without council support, what safeguards are there? How do we stop one person acting without proper checks?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: The proposals being consulted on would require major applications, including housing developments over 150 homes and commercial sites above a certain size, to be referred to the mayor. The mayor could leave a decision with the council, require changes or take it over. Another proposed power would let mayors reconsider council refusals for some schemes of more than 50 homes.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: One concern is that some of these decisions may be made entirely through written evidence, without an open meeting where residents or developers can speak. That could change after consultation. But a mayor would still have to follow planning law, provide sound reasons and face legal challenges or appeals if the decision was wrong.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: We also need proper written records showing how decisions were reached. Different mayors might otherwise adopt different standards. The Government should consider consistent safeguards, perhaps based on the system London already uses.

chapters.title: 6. Who Holds Mayors Accountable?
chapters.takeaway: Elected mayors can make responsibility clearer, but the witnesses disagree about whether every region should be required to adopt a mayoral system and how local government should be reorganised.

turns.speaker: Lord Razzall
turns.text: How clear is the relationship between a mayor and the wider regional authority? And how can voters hold these organisations accountable, especially in places that don't yet have an elected mayor?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: In Tees Valley, the law specifies which decisions belong to the mayor and which require the combined authority. But the legislation is complicated, and it's hard for ordinary people to understand. Some councillors appointed to regional committees also need better training about their responsibility to the whole region, rather than simply representing their own council.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: London has the London Assembly, which questions the mayor, investigates decisions and can overturn the mayor's budget with a two-thirds majority. The mayor regularly answers detailed questions in public. That, alongside elections every four years, provides a clear way to challenge decisions.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: We now have similar public questioning arrangements in Tees Valley, introduced relatively recently. So accountability is developing outside London too.

turns.speaker: Lord Razzall
turns.text: But if government increasingly directs funding towards regional mayors, what happens to areas that don't have one?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: That's a serious problem. Areas with mayors get better access to ministers, more funding opportunities and greater freedom. Some places have spent years failing to agree on whether to create a mayoralty, sometimes for political reasons. If government wants devolution everywhere, I think it may ultimately have to require areas to adopt it rather than wait for agreement.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: I'd favour encouraging areas by showing the advantages, rather than forcing them. There's value in local councils choosing to work together and creating something they support. That was an important part of how the original mayoral arrangements developed.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: But the practical result is still unequal. An area with a mayor can get more powers and money than one without. Unless that changes, places that don't agree to a mayor risk being left behind.

turns.speaker: Baroness Alexander of Cleveden
turns.text: The Government has recently halted plans to reorganise local government in England following legal advice. What does that mean for further devolution? Should the two changes happen together?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Reorganisation shouldn't delay more powers being given to existing mayors. They're separate questions. I understand why businesses would prefer a simpler, more consistent system across the country, because working out which authority does what can be difficult. But we shouldn't postpone useful changes while waiting for every area to have the same structure.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Previously, some areas had to reorganise their councils before getting a devolution deal. I don't know whether the Government is changing that policy. Allowing existing councils to form regional authorities without reorganising might speed things up, but it could also make responsibilities more confusing and increase the risk of powers being taken away from local councils.

chapters.title: 7. Do All Regions Have the Skills to Succeed?
chapters.takeaway: Different regions have very different staff, experience and economic opportunities, so greater local freedom alone won't guarantee that poorer areas can catch up.

turns.speaker: Lord Reid of Cardowan
turns.text: We've talked about unequal funding, but there's another problem. Some regional authorities have much more experience, expertise and staff than others. How can they compete fairly? And could stronger regional authorities end up taking skilled people away from local councils?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Teesside's experience shows why local knowledge matters. When the Redcar steelworks closed in 2015, around 3,500 people lost their jobs. Many eventually found other work, but that hid a serious problem. People who'd earned £70,000 or £80,000 were often taking insecure jobs paying £20,000 or £35,000. Simply saying they were employed again missed the loss of skills and living standards.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: We focused on industries that built Teesside's economy: chemicals, energy and large industrial projects. That experience is useful for newer industries too. For example, we're supporting BP and Equinor's £4 billion carbon capture and storage project. We can also use our existing engineering and construction skills to attract data centres and other energy-intensive businesses.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Having control over training budgets lets us help local people prepare for those jobs. Keeping the business rates from the former steelworks site is also crucial. We expect that site to generate around £250 million to £300 million a year in business rates for the regional authority by the end of the decade. That could provide substantial money for further investment.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: But even with all that progress, national decisions can undermine our work. Major investors depend on energy prices, tax policy and sometimes direct government support. The carbon capture project, for example, needed a government-backed financial agreement. Local freedom can achieve a great deal, but central government still controls decisions that can determine whether investments succeed.

turns.speaker: Lord Reid of Cardowan
turns.text: So returning to my question: do you accept that some authorities simply won't have the resources or expertise to make use of these powers as effectively as others?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Yes. Tees Valley has about 160 staff, while South Yorkshire has roughly 450 to 500. London is much larger and has decades more experience. Those differences affect how many projects an authority can manage and how quickly it can act. Even with more funding, we won't all begin with the same capabilities.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: That's true. London has a much larger organisation, particularly when you include Transport for London, policing and fire services. We have expertise other mayoral authorities are still developing, and we should help them build it. We're already working together across regions and political parties. If an overseas investor wants to develop an energy business better suited to Teesside, I'm happy to introduce them to Ben.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: I don't see London and Teesside as competitors. London competes internationally with places such as New York, Dubai and Singapore. We should use what each region does best, share our experience and help the whole country grow. That's one of the most promising things about giving regions more control.
